2027-07-09.title: Friday of the Fourteenth Week in Ordinary Time · St Augustine Zhao Rong and Companions, Martyrs
readings: I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again
The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord
I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves
2027-07-09.alt: Weekday of Ordinary Time, Week 14 (Year I). The optional memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the martyrs of China, may be kept; the readings are those of the weekday. The first reading is Jacob's journey into Egypt, the Gospel the warning of persecution in the mission discourse of St Matthew. Liturgical colour: green (red if the memorial is kept).
2027-07-09.verse: See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
theo: Jacob is an old man, and the journey he now takes is the hardest of his life. Joseph is alive and has sent wagons, and the whole family sets out for Egypt. But Egypt is not the land of the promise; it is a place where the patriarchs went in times of famine, and Isaac had once been forbidden to go there (Genesis 26:2). So at Beer-sheba, on the southern edge of Canaan, Jacob stops. He does not simply go. “When Israel set out on his journey with all that he had and came to Beer-sheba, he offered sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac.” And God answers: “God spoke to Israel in visions of the night, and said, ‘Jacob, Jacob.’ And he said, ‘Here I am.’” The double call is the call of the great vocations, the call of Abraham on Mount Moriah and of Moses at the burning bush. Then come three promises. “I am God, the God of your father; do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there.” That is the first: the promise of a people. “I myself will go down with you to Egypt.” That is the second: God himself will travel with him into the foreign land. “And I will also bring you up again; and Joseph's own hand shall close your eyes.” The third is the promise of a return, and of a gentle death in the arms of a son. So the whole house of Jacob goes down, sons, grandsons, daughters, little ones, flocks, in the wagons that Pharaoh sent; the chapter counts seventy persons, the seed of the people of God. At the end of the road comes the meeting. Israel sends Judah ahead to Goshen, and it is the man who once offered himself in place of Benjamin who leads the way. Then “Joseph made ready his chariot and went up to meet his father Israel in Goshen. He presented himself to him, fell on his neck, and wept on his neck a good while.” The father's first words are among the most moving in all the Bible: “I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive.” For more than twenty years he had grieved for a son he thought dead. Now he asks nothing more of life. The Psalm is the song of an old believer who has seen it all: “Trust in the Lord, and do good,” “Take delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart,” and the sweet promise that “in the days of famine they have abundance.” It ends: “The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord; he is their refuge in the time of trouble.”

In the Gospel the mission discourse takes a darker turn. Jesus does not promise his messengers an easy road: “See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.” The disciples must be shrewd, not naive, and pure, not cunning. They will be handed over to councils and flogged in the synagogues; they will be dragged before governors and kings “as a testimony to them and the Gentiles.” Even this is mission: a trial becomes a pulpit. Jesus promises help for exactly those moments: “When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.” The words about family betrayal are harsh: “Brother will betray brother to death, and a father his child.” In every age, in lands where the Church is persecuted, they have been true. “You will be hated by all because of my name. But the one who endures to the end will be saved.” Jesus also allows the prudent step: “When they persecute you in one town, flee to the next.” The martyr does not go looking for death; he goes on bearing witness, and if it comes, he does not run from it. The saying that closes the passage, “you will not have gone through all the towns of Israel before the Son of Man comes,” is a difficult one, read in several ways in the tradition of the Church; it tells at least that the work of the mission will not be finished before the Lord comes. The Church may keep today the memorial of St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the 120 martyrs of China whom Pope John Paul II canonised in the Jubilee Year 2000. Bishops, priests, religious and lay women and men, Chinese and foreign, they died for the faith in the centuries from 1648 to 1930. Augustine Zhao Rong was a Chinese priest who, according to the usual account, had first been a soldier guarding a captive missionary and was so moved by his faith that he asked for baptism; he died in prison in 1815. Closer to home, India too has her martyrs; St Devasahayam, a layman of the Tamil country who was killed in 1752 for his faith, was canonised in 2022. They show how Jacob's three promises hold good: God gives a people, he goes down with them into every foreign land, and he brings them up again.
outline: Ask: when did you last set out on a journey that frightened you, not knowing whether God was in it?
Point 1 · Do not be afraid to go down
At Beer-sheba God calls Jacob by name and promises to travel with him.
Father and son meet in Goshen: the tears of a lifetime.
Jesus warns the disciples of trials, and promises the Spirit's help.
The 120 martyrs of China and all who bear witness to the end.
“I myself will go down with you.”
live: Before any big decision or journey this week, stop and offer a prayer, as Jacob offered sacrifice at Beer-sheba, and ask God to go with you.
Pray for Christians who suffer for their faith, in China and elsewhere, and for those who persecute them, that they may come to know Christ.
2027-07-09.prayer: God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, you called Jacob by name at Beer-sheba and promised to go down with him into Egypt and bring him up again. Be with all who set out into the unknown this day, and with all who are afraid. Lord Jesus, you sent your disciples out like sheep among wolves and promised them the Spirit of your Father. Give us the wisdom of serpents and the innocence of doves; give us courage when we are brought before the powerful, and words from the Holy Spirit when we have none. Receive into your glory the martyrs of every land, St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, and the martyrs of India, and by their prayers keep us faithful to the end. Amen.
altar: Jacob offered sacrifices at Beer-sheba before he went down into Egypt, and received the promise of God's company on the road. Every Mass makes present the one sacrifice of Christ, to which all those earlier sacrifices pointed, and is a promise kept: “I am with you always, to the end of the age.” The early Christians were nourished by the Eucharist before they went to face the wolves; the word martyr means witness, and at Mass the Church remembers her martyrs by name in the Eucharistic Prayer and asks to be given a place with them. We receive the Lord's Body so that, like them, we may bear him into the world, by the way we live, even when it costs us something.

quick: God appears to Jacob at Beer-sheba and promises: I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again; Jacob and Joseph meet in Goshen with tears.
Psalm 37 sings the trust of the righteous, who have abundance even in famine, and whose salvation is from the Lord.
Jesus warns the Twelve that they go out like sheep among wolves, and promises that the Spirit of the Father will speak through them.
2027-07-09.action: Pray today by name for one Christian community that lives under pressure.
2027-07-09.question: Do I go into hard places with the confidence that God goes down with me?

family.explain: Old Jacob had to leave his home and go to a new country, and he was afraid. In the night God called him: Jacob, Jacob! And God said: do not be afraid. I will go with you. And God kept his promise. When Jacob saw Joseph again, he was so happy that he said: now I can die in peace! Jesus told his friends that it would not always be easy to follow him, but that the Holy Spirit would give them the words to say. Many brave Christians have died for Jesus. We call them martyrs.
family.intention: We pray for children and families who have to leave their homes, and for Christians who are in danger because they love Jesus.
family.ask: Ask: “When was the last time we were frightened about something new? How can we remember that God goes with us?”

illus: A young woman from a coastal village near Kochi once left for her first job in the Gulf, leaving behind a mother who had never been outside her district. At the airport her mother gave her a small card with a line from the Bible written in pencil: I myself will go down with you. The girl spent the first months in a crowded hostel, homesick and afraid. On the worst night she took out the card and read the line aloud, and she said it felt as though her mother's voice and God's voice were saying the same thing. Years later she put the same card into the hand of her own daughter on her first day at college. (An illustrative story.)

pm.open: God of Jacob, you go down with us into every foreign land. Lord Jesus, you promise us the Spirit when we are afraid. Be with us. Amen.
share: Jacob, Jacob. Here I am (Genesis 46:2). When has God called me by name, and how did I answer?
I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again (Genesis 46:4). Where do I most need to hear this promise in my own life?
I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive (Genesis 46:30). What would it take for me to be at peace in this way?
I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16). Where am I asked to be wise as a serpent and innocent as a dove?
pm.resp: The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord.
interc: For the Church in China and in every land where Christians are persecuted or restricted, that they may keep faith and hope.
For the martyrs of every age, St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, and St Devasahayam, that their witness may strengthen us.
For migrants and families who travel far from home, that they may know that God travels with them.
For elderly parents waiting to see their children again, that they may be given the gift of that meeting.
For our group, that the Spirit of the Father may speak through us when we are called to give an answer.
pm.close: Father, you go with your people into every land and you give your Spirit to those who witness to you. Keep us faithful to the end. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, Jacob is old, and he is afraid. He has to leave the land of the promise and go down to Egypt, a foreign country and the land of Pharaoh. And what does he do? He does what believers always do: before he sets out, he stops at Beer-sheba and offers sacrifice. And in the night God calls him: Jacob, Jacob. Here I am. And God says: do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there. I myself will go down with you (Genesis 46:3–4).

I myself will go down with you. That is one of the most beautiful sentences in the Bible. God does not wave from the shore. God goes down. Later God will go down in the Incarnation, in the womb of Mary, and down to the grave, and in the Mass he goes down on the altar. Wherever you go, whatever you fear, God goes down with you. And then the meeting of father and son: Joseph wept on his neck a good while, and old Jacob said: I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive (Genesis 46:30). A life that has seen God's faithfulness can be ended in peace.

In the Gospel Jesus speaks plainly to the Twelve: I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16). He does not hide it. Many of his followers have been put to death. Today the Church remembers St Augustine Zhao Rong and his companions, the martyrs of China. We think too of St Devasahayam, who gave his life for Christ in the south of our own land. How could they do it? Jesus had promised: it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you (Matthew 10:20).

Few of us will be asked to die for the faith. But all of us are asked to witness: at work, at home, in the family. To be wise as serpents and innocent as doves. To say a word for the Lord when it is not easy. Do not worry about how you are to speak. Go, trusting the God who said to Jacob: I myself will go down with you. Amen.
kids: Children, old Jacob was going to a new country, and he was afraid. But at night God called: Jacob, Jacob! And God said: do not be afraid, I will go with you. Later Jacob saw his son Joseph again, and he cried with joy. In the Gospel Jesus tells his friends that it will not always be easy to follow him, but the Holy Spirit will help them to find the right words. Some brave Christians, like the martyrs of China, died because they loved Jesus so much. When you feel afraid, say: Jesus, you are with me.

intro: Theme: “I myself will go down with you.”
Jacob goes down into Egypt with God's promise; Jesus sends his disciples as sheep among wolves, with the Spirit of the Father to speak in them.

points.h: Do not be afraid to go down
q: Then he said, “I am God, the God of your father; do not be afraid to go down to Egypt, for I will make of you a great nation there. I myself will go down with you to Egypt, and I will also bring you up again; and Joseph's own hand shall close your eyes.”
And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.
points.apply: Before the next frightening task or journey, say aloud: Lord, you go down with me.

sub: A life that has seen faithfulness.
q: Israel said to Joseph, “I can die now, having seen for myself that you are still alive.”
Master, now you are dismissing your servant in peace, according to your word;
points.apply: Call or visit an elderly person this week and listen to what God's faithfulness has meant in their life.

points.h: Sheep in the midst of wolves
q: The salvation of the righteous is from the Lord; he is their refuge in the time of trouble.
See, I am sending you out like sheep into the midst of wolves; so be wise as serpents and innocent as doves.
points.apply: Choose prudence and purity together in one real decision this week: neither naive nor cunning.

points.h: It is not you who speak
sub: The martyrs of China and of India.
q: Trust in the Lord, and do good; so you will live in the land, and enjoy security.

When they hand you over, do not worry about how you are to speak or what you are to say; for what you are to say will be given to you at that time; for it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father speaking through you.
points.apply: Learn the name of one martyr, and pray to them this week for the courage to bear witness.

concl: God calls Jacob by name, promises to go down with him into Egypt and to bring him up again, and so begins the long journey of a people.
Jesus sends his disciples like sheep among wolves and gives them the Spirit of the Father; the martyrs show that the promise holds.
2027-07-09.resolve: Offer one prayer before each important step this week, and pray for persecuted Christians by name.
